During her visit to Washington, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, discussed defence cooperation, support for Ukraine, the security situation in the Middle East, energy and joint action to counter threats posed by Russia and Iran with US and international partners. On 16-17 July 2026 in Washington, DC, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, met with US senators, participated in a ministerial meeting hosted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, met with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Israel, ministers from South American countries, as well as White House and US administration officials and the leaders of the Joint Baltic American National Committee (JBANC). During the meeting with Senators Elissa Slotkin, Gary Peters and Mark Kelly, the Minister highlighted the special bond between Latvia and the US and their close partnership in the field of defence. The Minister met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and participated in a ministerial meeting hosted by him, attended by representatives of more than 60 countries. In her address to the participants of the meeting, Baiba Braže shared Latvia's experience in strengthening resilience against the harmful influence and hybrid threats from foreign countries. The Minister emphasised that Russia and Iran are coordinating their actions more closely than ever, using sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, and proxy groups and criminal networks they support to weaken democratic countries. Countering these threats requires closer cooperation among allies, timely information sharing and coordinated action. Discussions with Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar focused on the security situation in the Middle East and efforts to prevent further escalation in the region. The ministers also exchanged views on the impact of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine on international security and continued support for Ukraine. During a meeting with the leaders of the Joint Baltic American National Committee (JBANC), cooperation in representing the interests of the Baltic states in the US and coordinated future joint activities were discussed. The Minister thanked the organisation's departing Managing Director, Karl Altau, for his contributions and expressed her commitment to working with the new Managing Director, Lee Allen. During the visit, meetings and discussions were also held with Jarrod Agen, Assistant to the President and Executive Director of the National Energy Dominance Council, as well as with representatives of the Department of Defence to discuss future cooperation in security, defence, energy and the economy.

https://www.dw.com/en/the-crash-of-a-ukr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iccw A Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft came down in a field about 100 meters from a border checkpoint with Romania Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP Advertisement When a drone entered Bulgaria 's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from. Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems. And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged. The Kardam border crossing (pictured here) is close to a Bulgarian compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable." Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident. What is known about the incident? At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania. Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field. In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives." Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged. Drone came down near gas pipeline The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine , and in close proximity to a Romanian station. This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target. Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low. Wake-up call for Bulgaria Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability. "Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT. While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania , these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach. Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though h e admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country. " Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last met at the NATO summit in Ankara in July Image: BGNES With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Was Russia involved? As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria. According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated. Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals. He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective. The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication. Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash. "The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case. As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine. Bulgaria has declined an invitation from French President Emmanuel Macron (center left) to join the Coalition of the Willing, which last met with Ukrainian representatives in Paris in July (seen here) Image: Tom Nicholson/AFP The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine. Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador. "This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position. A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party. While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy , promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine. Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine , blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing , which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine. "I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here." Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPA Ebola Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Agence France-Presse in Nairobi Tue 6 Oct 2026 05.35 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, after a Kenyan man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died after returning to the country. In mid-May, the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak, an extremely deadly disease that has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years. While Kenya has previously never reported a case, neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. The Kenyan citizen, who has not been named, fell ill about a month ago and had been treated in the DRC, Aden Duale, the Kenyan health minister, told reporters, before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Duale said the man was suffering “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”. He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, saying that he “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT). Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”. However, he added that authorities were pursuing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said. Duale said that arrangements for a “safe and dignified burial” of the man were planned for later in the day in line with public health standards. He did not disclose further details. As of 2 October, the World Health Organization had recorded 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases since the emergence in the DRC of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment. After starting in the north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the north and east. DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak Read more The virus has hit unstable regions in the vast central African country where armed clashes and violence, alongside a critical lack of resources, have hindered the health response. The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year for the creation of an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.
